title: One main verb to a clause
why: 10 of your 18 Standard English Conventions misses come down to this one rule — 5 of them because you picked a main verb where the sentence already had one.
rule: One clause, one main verb — unless “and” joins a second.
ruleDetail: The main verb is the one carrying the tense — past, present or future. Once the subject has it, the blank cannot be a second one. It becomes a describing form instead: -ing, -ed, or to + verb.

forms.example: This hypothesis, suggesting the trees survived, cannot stand.
The bridge, designed by Roebling, still stands.
She paused to consider the map.

formsWarning: Careful with -ed: it is spelled the same as the past tense. "They published a study" is a main verb; "the study, published in 2023, showed…" is a describing form. The spelling will not tell you which. Only the rest of the sentence will.
steps: Find the subject. Who is doing the action?
Read all the way to the full stop.
Look for another main verb belonging to that subject.
then: No other main verb — the blank IS the main verb. Use the tensed form, and check it agrees with the subject.
There is one already — the blank is a describing form. Use -ing, -ed or to + verb.
trap: The wrong answer sounds perfect at the blank, because it completes the sentence so far. That is exactly why it is offered. The words that prove it wrong sit later — in 4 of your 5 errors, 10 or more words later. Don't decide at the blank. Read to the full stop.

exception.title: The one exception: and
exception.intro: When “and” joins two verbs, they share the subject and the clause is allowed both.

pairs.right: Scientists studied the data and published their findings.
The lock would increase the salinity and create a barrier.
pairs.wrong: The lock would increase the salinity and creates a barrier.

exception.note: With a modal — would, could, will, might, should — the modal carries the tense for both verbs, so the second stays in its plain form: create, not creates. You missed exactly this on Practice Test 8, Module 1, Question 20.

commas: Commas are a separate question, and not every describing phrase takes them. Ask what the phrase is doing. If it picks out which one you mean, it runs on with no commas: “The student sitting by the window answered first.” If it is extra information dropped in, it is fenced at both ends: “Priya, sitting by the window, answered first.” Your two examples below are one of each — College Board calls the first a restrictive phrase and the second a supplementary one.

examples.sentence: This hypothesis ___ that certain trees, such as P. sylvestris, survived without interruption throughout the Holocene cannot stand, researchers Michael O'Connell and Karen Molloy counter.
choices: suggesting
suggested
suggests
has suggested
examples.working: Subject: this hypothesis. Read to the full stop and there it is — cannot stand. That is already its main verb, so the blank cannot be a second one. "This hypothesis suggests" sounds perfect; the words that sink it are 11 further on. No commas here: the phrase says which hypothesis, so it runs straight on — restrictive.

examples.sentence: American abstract artist Richard ___ his installations to make passersby keenly aware of how one's movements are affected by their environment, assembles large-scale steel plates into sculptures.
choices: Serra is intending
Serra, intends
Serra, intending
Serra intends
examples.wrong: Richard Serra intends his installations … , assembles steel plates.
examples.right: Richard Serra, intending his installations … , assembles steel plates.
examples.working: Subject: Richard Serra. His main verb is assembles, at the far end, so the middle is describing him. This one is extra information rather than which-one, so it is fenced at both ends — and the comma after "environment" is already printed for you, which tells you the other belongs after "Serra".

examples.sentence: In January 2023, Nery and her colleagues ___ a study showing changes over time in four whale genes associated with body size.
choices: published
publishing
having published
to publish
examples.wrong: Nery and her colleagues publishing a study.
examples.right: Nery and her colleagues published a study.
examples.working: The same test, the other way round. Cover the blank, read to the full stop: there is no other main verb anywhere. So the blank has to be it. This is the case that stops the rule collapsing into "always pick -ing" — the other three choices leave the sentence with no verb at all.

memorise: Find the subject → cover the blank → read to the full stop.
No main verb yet? The blank is the main verb.
Main verb already there? The blank is a describing form: -ing, -ed, to + verb.
Don't decide at the blank. Read to the full stop.

title: Function, not content
why: 13 of your 96 missed questions are this one type — "which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion" — and 12 of the 13 are the same question word for word. The wrong ones you took describe what the underlined part SAYS. The answer describes what it DOES in relation to the text around it.
rule: Ask what it does, not what it says.
ruleDetail: CONTENT = what it says. FUNCTION = what it does. The underlined part is not being tested by itself. Ask what job it does in the passage: does it add a detail, admit a limitation, introduce an idea, or support a claim?

forms.form: talks about the text around it
forms.example: adds detail to the previous sentence · admits a limitation · supports the claim · introduces an example

forms.form: just tells you what the words say
forms.example: describes the desert · tells what the study found · recounts a moment

formsWarning: Don't judge a choice by its first verb. "Explains" is right when it explains how the underlined part connects to the passage, and wrong when it only tells you what the underlined words say. Your own misses show describes, explains, presents, provides and recounts are the common trap openings — use that as a tiebreaker, never as the rule.
steps: Cover the underlined part. Could you still write the choice?
Yes → it probably describes content. Reject it.
No → it describes a job. Keep checking.
then: Now check the choice is actually supported by the passage.
trap: The trap is often TRUE. That is why it is tempting. It answers "what does this say?" instead of "what does this do?" — accurate about the underlined words, silent about their job.

examples.source: Practice 6, Module 2, Question 5 — and you missed the same question again on paper Test 6
examples.sentence: …his style underwent an abrupt transformation. [Turning away from landscapes painted in an expressionist style … Johnson began painting portraits of Black Americans in a bold new way.] Evocative of African sculpture …
choices: It elaborates on the previous sentence's statement about a transitional moment in Johnson's artistic career.
It provides information about Johnson's travels in support of a claim about his artistic influences.
It recounts a moment in Johnson's personal life that enabled the success of his subsequent career.
It presents evidence that calls into question the previous sentence's characterization of Johnson's development.
examples.answer: It elaborates on the previous sentence's statement about a transitional moment in Johnson's artistic career.
examples.wrong: It provides information about Johnson's travels…
examples.right: It elaborates on the previous sentence's statement…
examples.working: The sentence before says his style "underwent an abrupt transformation". The underlined sentence then says what the transformation was: away from expressionist landscapes, towards portraits. That is elaboration — it takes the previous claim and fills it in. Your choice, "provides information about Johnson's travels", describes content, and points at nothing. Note also that the answer names the previous sentence out loud. Three of your 13 answers did that; not one of the traps did.

examples.sentence: …most medieval towns had at least one public bathhouse … [While such amenities were available mainly to town dwellers,] regular bathing in rivers and streams or daily sponge baths at home were common practices throughout medieval Europe.
choices: It asserts that steam baths were more popular in rural areas than in urban ones.
It describes a limitation of earlier historians' studies of medieval bathing habits.
It concedes that not all people in medieval Europe had access to public bathhouses.
It explains why Janega decided to study the popularity of public bathhouses.
examples.answer: It concedes that not all people in medieval Europe had access to public bathhouses.
examples.wrong: It asserts that steam baths were more popular in rural areas…
examples.right: It concedes that not all people had access to public bathhouses.
examples.working: The whole text argues medieval people were cleaner than we assume. This clause admits something that cuts against that argument — not everyone could reach a bathhouse — before the rest of the sentence answers it. Admitting a point against your own case is conceding, and that is a job. Your choice asserts a fact about rural popularity, which the text never claims and which does nothing for the argument either way.

examples.sentence: Seira et al. … found that the messages had only small and short-lived effects on behavior. Seira et al. asserted that such effects may nevertheless be worth pursuing, [given the negligible cost of messaging.]
choices: It notes a factor that led Seira et al. to not dismiss risk-disclosure messaging altogether.
It acknowledges a type of messaging Seira et al. may not have fully considered.
It describes a consideration that explains why Seira et al. recommended risk-disclosure requirements.
It points out a circumstance that Seira et al. conceded may weaken messaging.
examples.answer: It notes a factor that led Seira et al. to not dismiss risk-disclosure messaging altogether.
examples.wrong: It describes a consideration that explains why they recommended requirements…
examples.right: It notes a factor that led them not to dismiss messaging altogether.
examples.working: Six words underlined. You physically cannot answer this from the underlined portion — the whole answer is in what surrounds it. The researchers found the messages barely worked, then said they were worth doing anyway; these six words are the reason that survives the bad result. Note the trap here opens with "describes a consideration that explains" — content vocabulary, on a question where the underlined text has almost no content of its own.

memorise: Read before + after. Ask: WHY IS THIS HERE?
Cover the underlined words. Could you still write the choice? Yes → probably content. Reject it.
The answer describes the JOB: elaborates, concedes, supports, introduces, illustrates.
check: True ≠ correct. Job first, truth second.
